# Angiotensin Receptor–Neprilysin Inhibition in Heart Failure: A Narrative Review

## Rationale and pharmacology

Heart failure (HF) management has long centred on antagonising the deleterious neurohormonal pathways—chiefly the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system (RAAS) and sympathetic nervous system—that drive progressive ventricular remodelling [1]. A complementary, counter-regulatory axis is the natriuretic peptide system. Natriuretic peptides promote natriuresis, vasodilation and inhibition of cardiac remodelling, and suppress RAAS and adrenergic activity [2]. These peptides are degraded by neprilysin, a neutral endopeptidase, making the enzyme an attractive therapeutic target [2]. However, neprilysin also degrades other vasoactive substrates including angiotensin II and bradykinin, which explains why neprilysin inhibition is most rationally combined with RAAS blockade [2].

This concept was first tested with the vasopeptidase inhibitor omapatrilat, which combined ACE and neprilysin inhibition. In the OVERTURE trial of 5770 patients, 5770 patients with New York Heart Association class II to IV heart failure were randomly assigned to enalapril or the ACE-NEP inhibitor omapatrilat for a mean of 14.5 months. The OVERTURE trial demonstrated that omapatrilat reduced morbidity and mortality but was not more effective than ACE inhibition alone [3]. Critically, dual ACE/neprilysin inhibition raised bradykinin excessively, increasing angioedema risk and precluding approval [4]. Combining neprilysin inhibition with an angiotensin-receptor blocker (rather than an ACE inhibitor) circumvented this problem, yielding sacubitril/valsartan (LCZ696), the first angiotensin receptor–neprilysin inhibitor (ARNI) [5].

## Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction

The pivotal PARADIGM-HF trial compared sacubitril/valsartan with enalapril in ambulatory patients with HF and reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) [5]. In PARADIGM-HF, the angiotensin receptor neprilysin inhibitor sacubitril/valsartan was more effective than the angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor enalapril in patients with heart failure and reduced ejection fraction [5]. The sacubitril/valsartan versus enalapril hazard ratio for the primary composite end point was 0.80, and for cardiovascular death was 0.80 [6]. Benefit was consistent regardless of background therapy [6], and beyond hard outcomes, sacubitril/valsartan also reduced clinical progression: fewer LCZ696-treated patients required intensification of medical treatment for heart failure or an emergency department visit for worsening heart failure [7].

Mechanistic studies have helped explain these benefits. In PROVE-HF, treatment with sacubitril/valsartan reduced NT-proBNP, and reduction in NT-proBNP concentration was weakly yet significantly correlated with improvements in markers of cardiac volume and function at 12 months, suggesting reverse cardiac remodelling [8]. In contrast, the EVALUATE-HF trial found no significant difference in the change in aortic characteristic impedance (a measure of central aortic stiffness) at 12 weeks among patients treated with sacubitril-valsartan vs enalapril, indicating that the clinical benefits are not mediated by reduced arterial stiffness [9].

## Initiation in acute and de novo heart failure

Because PARADIGM-HF enrolled stable outpatients, the safety of initiation during hospitalisation was uncertain [10]. The PIONEER-HF trial addressed this in patients stabilised after acute decompensated HFrEF [11]. The time-averaged reduction in the NT-proBNP concentration was significantly greater in the sacubitril–valsartan group than in the enalapril group [11], and an exploratory composite of clinical events also favoured ARNI [12], without excess renal dysfunction, hyperkalaemia or hypotension [10]. The open-label TRANSITION study confirmed feasibility of in-hospital or early post-discharge initiation in haemodynamically stabilised patients [13]. Notably, many patients in these trials were ACE-inhibitor/ARB-naïve [14], supporting ARNI use even in de novo presentations.

## Heart failure with preserved and mildly reduced ejection fraction

The phase 2 PARAMOUNT trial first signalled efficacy beyond HFrEF: in patients with EF ≥45%, the study met its primary endpoint, demonstrating a 23% greater reduction in NT-proBNP at 12 weeks for LCZ696 compared with valsartan [15]. The definitive PARAGON-HF trial, however, narrowly missed significance: the primary endpoint of total HF hospitalisations or cardiovascular death was narrowly missed (HR 0.87, CI 0.75–1.01; P = 0.059) [16]. Subgroup analyses suggested benefit was concentrated among patients at the lower end of the EF spectrum and in women [16,17]. A pooled, patient-level analysis across the EF spectrum reinforced this: while overall benefit was observed comparing sacubitril/valsartan to RAS inhibition, the findings were driven by benefit in patients with LVEF below the normal range, whereas patients at the highest end of the ejection fraction range did not appear to benefit [18]. The PARAGLIDE-HF trial extended testing to patients with EF >40% and a recent worsening HF event [19], and a pre-specified pooled analysis with PARAGON-HF showed that sacubitril/valsartan significantly reduced total worsening HF events and cardiovascular death in those with recent worsening HF [20].

## Guideline recommendations and practical considerations

These data are reflected in contemporary guidelines. The 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA guideline established ARNI, beta-blockers, MRAs and SGLT2 inhibitors as foundational therapy for HFrEF [21], where ARNI are recommended (Class 1A) as the preferred renin–angiotensin modulator in HFrEF [22]. For HF with mildly reduced or preserved EF, recommendations for ARNI are weaker (Class 2b) [23]. The 2021 ESC guideline similarly recommends replacing an ACE inhibitor/ARB with sacubitril/valsartan in symptomatic HFrEF, while noting that initiation in ACE-I naïve (de novo) patients may be considered, and patients commenced on sacubitril/valsartan should have adequate blood pressure and an eGFR ≥30 mL/min/1.73 m² [24,25]. A 36-hour washout after ACE-inhibitor therapy is required to mitigate angioedema risk [10].

Practical caveats remain. Symptomatic hypotension is more frequent with ARNI than comparators, particularly in HFpEF populations and those with low baseline systolic pressure [26]. Lower-than-target doses still confer benefit relative to comparator [27], and a starting dose of 24/26 mg twice daily is available for cautious initiation [25]. Real-world tolerability data from high-risk hospitalised patients have been reassuring [28].

## Conclusion

ARNI therapy represents a major therapeutic advance for HFrEF, with robust mortality and morbidity benefits, favourable reverse remodelling, and safety across acute and de novo settings [5,8,11]. Its role in higher-EF phenotypes is more nuanced, with benefit attenuating as EF rises above normal [18]. Ongoing evidence continues to refine optimal patient selection, dosing strategies, and integration with the other pillars of guideline-directed therapy [21,29,30].
